claim: NCLX (SLC8B1) mRNA levels are significantly downregulated in colon and rectal adenocarcinoma (COADREAD) tumors compared to adjacent normal tissue according to TCGA database analysis.
source: Using the publicly available Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database, we found that NCLX (SLC8B1) mRNA levels were significantly downregulated in both colon and rectal adenocarcinoma (COADREAD) tumors as compared to the adjacent normal tissue (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by TCGA database analysis and shown in Figure 1A

claim: SLC8B1 mRNA levels are substantially reduced to near loss in colorectal tumor samples from Penn State University Medical Center patients compared to paired normal adjacent tissues.
source: Consistent with the TCGA data, we observed a substantial reduction to a near loss in SLC8B1 mRNA in colorectal tumor samples isolated from patients undergoing surgery at Penn State University Medical Center as compared to the paired normal adjacent tissues (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from patient samples shown in Figure 1B

claim: There is no difference in SLC8B1 mRNA levels between male and female tumor tissues.
source: There was no difference in SLC8B1 mRNA levels between male and female tumor tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: There is no difference in SLC8B1 mRNA levels between patients bearing mutated and normal proto-oncogene KRAS and phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3K).
source: There was no difference in SLC8B1 mRNA levels between male and female tumor tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and between patients bearing mutated and normal proto-oncogene KRAS and phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3K) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1C

claim: Low NCLX expression is associated with TP53 mutations in colorectal tumors.
source: However, low NCLX expression was associated with TP53 mutations and wild type BRAF tumors (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: Low NCLX expression is associated with wild type BRAF tumors.
source: However, low NCLX expression was associated with TP53 mutations and wild type BRAF tumors (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: SLC8B1 mRNA is appreciably reduced in CRC patients of all age groups according to TCGA data analysis from UALCAN.
source: TCGA data analysis from UALCAN (Chandrashekar et al., 2017) revealed that SLC8B1 mRNA was appreciably reduced in CRC patients of all age groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis from UALCAN database shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Both adenocarcinoma and mucinous adenocarcinoma have a significant reduction in SLC8B1 mRNA levels compared to normal tissue.
source: Both adenocarcinoma and mucinous adenocarcinoma had a significant reduction in SLC8B1 mRNA levels as compared to the normal tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: There is a significant loss of NCLX in adenomas with malignant transformation from stage I through stage IV.
source: Subsequent analysis revealed a significant loss of NCLX in adenomas with malignant transformation from stage I through stage IV (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: There is a significant reduction in SLC8B1 mRNA level in late-stage (stage III and IV) colorectal tumors compared to early-stage (stages I and II) tumors from the TCGA database.
source: There was a significant reduction in SLC8B1 mRNA level in late-stage (stage III and IV) colorectal tumors as compared to early-stage (stages I and II) tumors from the TCGA database (Figure 1E,F)
evidence: Supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1E and 1F

claim: Patient samples from Penn State University Medical Center show a significant reduction in SLC8B1 mRNA level in late-stage tumors compared to early-stage tumors.
source: There was a significant reduction in SLC8B1 mRNA level in late-stage (stage III and IV) colorectal tumors as compared to early-stage (stages I and II) tumors from the TCGA database (Figure 1E,F), with similar results when we analyzed the patient samples obtained from Penn State University Medical Center (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from patient samples shown in Figure 1G

claim: NCLX expression is significantly downregulated in CRC specimens.
source: Together, these results show that NCLX expression is significantly downregulated in CRC specimens, and that NCLX loss correlates with late-stage colorectal adenocarcinomas.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple data analyses including TCGA and patient samples

claim: NCLX loss correlates with late-stage colorectal adenocarcinomas.
source: Together, these results show that NCLX expression is significantly downregulated in CRC specimens, and that NCLX loss correlates with late-stage colorectal adenocarcinomas.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from TCGA and patient sample analyses showing reduced NCLX in late-stage tumors

claim: NCLX KO mice have approximately 50% fewer tumors than littermate control mice in the AOM-DSS colitis-associated colorectal cancer model.
source: Although there is a clear association between NCLX loss and CRC in TCGA data, the colons of NCLX KO mice displayed approximately 50% less tumors than those of littermate control mice (Figure 1I,J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by tumor count data from AOM-DSS mouse model shown in Figure 1I and 1J

claim: Tumors that developed in the colons of NCLX KO mice are markedly smaller than those in the colons of littermate control mice.
source: Further, the tumors that developed in the colons of NCLX KO mice were markedly smaller than those in the colons of littermate control mice, as determined by measurements of tumor size (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by tumor size measurements shown in Figure 1K

claim: Histological analyses reveal significantly reduced dysplasia in the colons of NCLX KO mice compared with colons from littermate control mice.
source: Histological analyses of colon tissues revealed significantly reduced dysplasia in the colons of NCLX KO mice compared with colons from littermate control mice (Figure 1L,M).
evidence: Supported by histology data shown in Figure 1L and 1M

claim: There is a significant reduction in the total luciferase bioluminescence flux in mice xenografted with HCT116 NCLX KO cells compared to HCT116 control-injected mice.
source: There was a significant reduction in the total luciferase bioluminescence flux in mice xenografted with HCT116 NCLX KO cells by comparison to the HCT116 control-injected mice (Figure 2B,C), indicating that the loss of NCLX in CRC cells caused reduced tumor growth.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figure 2B and 2C

claim: Loss of NCLX in CRC cells causes reduced tumor growth in xenograft models.
source: There was a significant reduction in the total luciferase bioluminescence flux in mice xenografted with HCT116 NCLX KO cells by comparison to the HCT116 control-injected mice (Figure 2B,C), indicating that the loss of NCLX in CRC cells caused reduced tumor growth.
evidence: Inferred from bioluminescence data showing reduced flux in NCLX KO xenografts

claim: Primary tumor volumes in the spleens of HCT116 NCLX KO-injected mice are significantly reduced compared to control HCT116-injected mice at six weeks.
source: Similarly, the primary tumor volumes (at the time of sacrifice, at six weeks) in the spleens of HCT116 NCLX KO-injected mice were significantly reduced compared to control HCT116-injected mice (Figure 2D,E), consistent with the in vivo tumor growth in the AOM-DSS model.
evidence: Supported by primary tumor volume measurements shown in Figure 2D and 2E

claim: SCID mice injected with HCT116 NCLX KO cells show strikingly increased metastasis to the liver and colon compared to control HCT116-injected mice at Week 6.
source: Interestingly, SCID mice injected with the HCT116 NCLX KO cells showed strikingly increased metastasis (Figure 2B), specifically to the liver and colon as compared to control HCT116-injected mice at the time of sacrifice (Week 6; Figure 2F–H).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence and tissue imaging data shown in Figure 2B, 2F, 2G, and 2H

claim: No metastasis to the lung, heart or brain was observed in mice of both groups in the xenograft model.
source: We did not observe any metastasis to the lung, heart or brain of mice of both groups in this xenograft model.
evidence: Direct observation from xenograft experiments

claim: SCID mice with intra-splenic injection of HCT116 NCLX KO cells have reduced overall survival compared to mice injected with control HCT116 cells.
source: Significantly, the SCID mice with intra-splenic injection of HCT116 NCLX KO cells had reduced overall survival compared to mice injected with control HCT116 cells (Figure 2I), suggesting that increased CRC metastasis is the primary cause of lethality in the HCT116 NCLX KO xenograft model.
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 2I

claim: Increased CRC metastasis is the primary cause of lethality in the HCT116 NCLX KO xenograft model.
source: Significantly, the SCID mice with intra-splenic injection of HCT116 NCLX KO cells had reduced overall survival compared to mice injected with control HCT116 cells (Figure 2I), suggesting that increased CRC metastasis is the primary cause of lethality in the HCT116 NCLX KO xenograft model.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between increased metastasis and reduced survival in NCLX KO xenografts

claim: Loss of NCLX causes reduced primary tumor growth with increased metastatic progression of colorectal cancer.
source: Altogether, our results show that loss of NCLX causes reduced primary tumor growth with increased metastatic progression of colorectal cancer.
evidence: Summary conclusion from both AOM-DSS and xenograft model data

claim: A significant reduction in proliferation is observed in NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells.
source: A significant reduction in proliferation was observed in NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by CyQUANT proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: Transient knockdown of NCLX using shRNA reduces HCT116 cell proliferation.
source: Similarly, transient knockdown of NCLX (NCLX KD) using shRNA reduced HCT116 cell proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J

claim: There is a significant increase in cleaved caspase-3 protein in HCT116 NCLX KO clones compared to control HCT116 cells, suggesting an increase in apoptosis.
source: We observed significant increase in cleaved caspase-3 protein using immunofluorescence staining in HCT116 NCLX KO clones as compared to control HCT116 cells, suggesting an increase in apoptosis of NCLX KO CRC cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K,L).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K and 1L

claim: The reduced tumor sizes observed in vivo due to NCLX knockout are likely a consequence of reduced CRC cell proliferation and increased apoptosis.
source: These data suggest that the reduced tumor sizes observed in vivo (Figures 1 and 2) due to NCLX knockout are likely a consequence of reduced CRC cell proliferation and increased apoptosis.
evidence: Inferred from proliferation and apoptosis data in NCLX KO cells

claim: All NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells have a marked increase in migration at 24 hr.
source: A gap closure assay revealed that all NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 cells (Figure 3C,D) and DLD1 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1J light colors) had a marked increase in migration at 24 hr.
evidence: Supported by gap closure assay data shown in Figure 3C, 3D, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1J

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of NCLX in HCT116 cells causes a significant increase in cell migration at 12 and 24 hr time points.
source: Similar to knockout, shRNA-mediated knockdown of NCLX in HCT116 cells also caused a significant increase in cell migration at 12 and 24 hr time points (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by gap closure assay data shown in Figure 3E and 3F

claim: At 6 hr, there is a significant increase in migration of NCLX KO #33 cells compared to HCT116 control cells.
source: At 6 hr, we observed a significant increase in migration of NCLX KO #33 cells as compared to HCT116 control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M).
evidence: Supported by gap closure assay data at 6 hr shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1M

claim: The increased cell migration of HCT116 NCLX KO cells is preserved in the presence of the cytostatic compound mitomycin C at 12 hr and 24 hr time points.
source: Effects of proliferation on cell migration were further ruled out by documenting that the increased cell migration of HCT116 NCLX KO cells is preserved in the presence of the cytostatic compound, mitomycin C at 12 hr and 24 hr time points (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: Supported by gap closure assay data with mitomycin C treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1N

claim: A marked increase in invasion is observed in all NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 compared to their respective controls.
source: Further, the invasive behavior of NCLX KO cells was determined using a Matrigel-coated Boyden chamber assay. A marked increase in invasion was observed in all NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 as compared to their respective controls (Figure 3G,H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: Supported by Matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 3G, 3H, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1O

claim: mRNA levels of MMP1, MMP2, and MMP9 are significantly upregulated in all HCT116 NCLX KO clones compared to control HCT116 cells.
source: Supporting this invasive phenotype are our observations that mRNA levels of the matrix metalloproteinases MMP1, 2, and 9 were significantly upregulated in all the HCT116 NCLX KO clones, as compared to control HCT116 cells (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3I, 3J, and 3K

claim: Protein levels of MMP1, MMP2, and MMP9 are significantly increased in NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells.
source: Similarly, the protein levels of MMP1, 2, and 9 were also significantly increased in NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells (Figure 3L,M, Figure 3—figure supplement 1P,Q).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3L, 3M, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1P, 1Q

claim: The activity of MMP2 and MMP9 is markedly increased in all NCLX KO clones of HCT116 cells compared to control HCT116 cells.
source: We then tested the MMPs activity using zymography and revealed that the activity of MMP2 and 9 were markedly increased in all the NCLX KO clones of HCT116 cells compared to control HCT116 cells (Figure 3N,O).
evidence: Supported by zymography data shown in Figure 3N and 3O

claim: The loss of NCLX expression in CRC cells mostly contributes to post-transcriptional regulation of MMPs.
source: This was more prominent than changes observed at the mRNA and protein levels, suggesting that the loss of NCLX expression in CRC cells mostly contributes to post-transcriptional regulation of MMPs.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of MMP activity changes versus mRNA and protein level changes

claim: Loss of NCLX in CRC cells causes an increase in migration and invasion through increased MMP1, 2, and 9 protein levels and activity.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the loss of NCLX in CRC cells causes an increase in migration and invasion of CRC cells through increased MMP1, 2, and 9 protein levels and activity.
evidence: Summary conclusion from migration, invasion, and MMP data

claim: All NCLX KO clones show a significant reduction in mtCa2+ extrusion with no significant change in the rate of mtCa2+ uptake.
source: All NCLX KO clones showed a significant reduction in mtCa2+ extrusion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–L) with no significant change in the rate of mtCa2+ uptake.
evidence: Supported by Rhod-2 AM mitochondrial calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–L

claim: HCT116, DLD1, and HT29 cells transfected with siRNA against NCLX exhibit a significant reduction in mtCa2+ extrusion with no significant change in mtCa2+ uptake.
source: Similar to the NCLX KO cells, HCT116 cells, DLD1 cells, and HT29 cells transfected with siRNA against NCLX (siNCLX) exhibited a significant reduction in mtCa2+ extrusion with no significant change in mtCa2+ uptake (Figure 4—figure supplement 1N–V).
evidence: Supported by Rhod-2 AM mitochondrial calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1N–V

claim: Inhibition of mtCa2+ extrusion through NCLX knockdown in several cell types leads to the inhibition of plasma membrane ORAI1 channels, reduced Ca2+ entry from the extracellular space, and decreased cytosolic Ca2+.
source: We previously showed that inhibition of mtCa2+ extrusion through NCLX knockdown in several cell types leads to the inhibition of plasma membrane ORAI1 channels, reduced Ca2+ entry from the extracellular space, and decreased cytosolic Ca2+ (Ben-Kasus Nissim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Ben-Kasus Nissim et al., 2017

claim: NCLX KO cells show a reduction in Ca2+ entry with no effect on Ca2+ release from the ER.
source: Therefore, we measured cytosolic Ca2+ in response to stimulation with ATP in HCT116 cells and their NCLX KO #33 counterparts using the dye Fura-2 and showed a reduction in Ca2+ entry in NCLX KO cells with no effect on Ca2+ release from the ER (Figure 4—figure supplement 1W,X).
evidence: Supported by Fura-2 cytosolic calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1W and 1X

claim: Inhibition of NCLX function in CRC cell lines leads to enhanced mitochondrial matrix Ca2+ concentration due to reduced mtCa2+ extrusion and to decreased cytosolic Ca2+ due to reduced Ca2+ entry across the plasma membrane.
source: Collectively, these results show that inhibition of NCLX function in CRC cell lines leads to enhanced mitochondrial matrix Ca2+ concentration due to reduced mtCa2+ extrusion and to decreased cytosolic Ca2+ due to reduced Ca2+ entry across the plasma membrane.
evidence: Summary conclusion from mitochondrial and cytosolic calcium measurements

claim: There is a significant decrease in the accumulation of TMRE in NCLX KO cells, indicating that mitochondria of NCLX KO cells are more depolarized than control HCT116 and DLD1 cells.
source: We observed a significant decrease in the accumulation of TMRE in NCLX KO cells, indicating that mitochondria of NCLX KO cells are more depolarized than control HCT116 and DLD1 cells (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by TMRE flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A and 4B

claim: 60–70% of mitochondria in NCLX KO CRC clones show altered shape and disrupted cristae compared to control cells.
source: Examining mitochondrial structure using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging revealed that 60–70% of mitochondria in NCLX KO CRC clones showed altered shape and disrupted cristae compared to control cells (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by TEM imaging data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: Mitochondrial membranes and cristae of NCLX KO clones of HCT116 and DLD1 cells are disrupted.
source: We discovered that mitochondrial membranes and cristae of the NCLX KO clones of HCT116 and DLD1 cells were disrupted (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by TEM imaging data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C

claim: Overall mitochondrial area is not changed in NCLX KO clones.
source: Specifically, while overall mitochondrial area was not changed in NCLX KO clones (Figure 4D), we observed a greater number of mitochondria with disordered cristae (Figure 4E) and a decrease in the number of intact cristae per mitochondrion (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by TEM quantification data shown in Figure 4D

claim: There is a greater number of mitochondria with disordered cristae in NCLX KO clones.
source: Specifically, while overall mitochondrial area was not changed in NCLX KO clones (Figure 4D), we observed a greater number of mitochondria with disordered cristae (Figure 4E) and a decrease in the number of intact cristae per mitochondrion (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by TEM quantification data shown in Figure 4E

claim: There is a decrease in the number of intact cristae per mitochondrion in NCLX KO clones.
source: Specifically, while overall mitochondrial area was not changed in NCLX KO clones (Figure 4D), we observed a greater number of mitochondria with disordered cristae (Figure 4E) and a decrease in the number of intact cristae per mitochondrion (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by TEM quantification data shown in Figure 4F

claim: There is a significant increase in autophagic vesicles in NCLX KO cells compared to control HCT116 cells.
source: We also observed a significant increase in autophagic vesicles in NCLX KO cells compared to control HCT116 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by TEM quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D

claim: The autophagy/mitophagy vesicle marker LC3BII is significantly increased in all NCLX KO clones of HCT116 and DLD1 cells.
source: The autophagy/mitophagy vesicle marker LC3BII was significantly increased in all NCLX KO clones of HCT116 and DLD1 cells (Figure 4G,H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4G, 4H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F, 2G

claim: The levels of the p62 protein are increased in all NCLX KO clones of HCT116 and DLD1 cells.
source: Interestingly, the levels of the p62 protein, a signaling molecule that is downstream of LC3BII that is degraded on induction of autophagy (Liu et al., 2016; Youle and Narendra, 2011), were also increased in all the NCLX KO clones of HCT116 and DLD1 cells (Figure 4G,I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4G, 4I, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F, 2G

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of NCLX in HCT116 results in increased LC3BII and p62 protein levels.
source: Similarly, the shRNA-mediated knockdown of NCLX in HCT116 (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1I for evidence of SLC8B1 mRNA knockdown using shRNA) resulted in increased LC3BII and p62 protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H,I).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2H and 2I

claim: There is a significant reduction in maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity in NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells.
source: We observed a significant reduction in maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity in NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cell (Figure 4J–M, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2J–M).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR data shown in Figure 4J–M and Figure 4—figure supplement 2J–M

claim: Basal respiration and ATP generation are significantly reduced in DLD1 NCLX KO clones.
source: Interestingly, basal respiration and ATP generation were significantly reduced in DLD1 NCLX KO clones, and remained mostly unaltered in HCT116 NCLX KO clones as compared to their respective controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 2J–M, and Figure 4J–M).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR data shown in Figure 4J–M and Figure 4—figure supplement 2J–M

claim: Basal respiration and ATP generation remain mostly unaltered in HCT116 NCLX KO clones compared to controls.
source: Interestingly, basal respiration and ATP generation were significantly reduced in DLD1 NCLX KO clones, and remained mostly unaltered in HCT116 NCLX KO clones as compared to their respective controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 2J–M, and Figure 4J–M).
evidence: Supported by Seahorse OCR data shown in Figure 4J–M and Figure 4—figure supplement 2J–M

claim: There is no significant change in the expression of mitochondrial respiratory Complex components I–V between HCT116 cells and their NCLX KO clones.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe any significant change in the expression of any of the above described components of the mitochondrial respiratory Complexes I–V between HCT116 cells and their NCLX KO clones (Figure 4—figure supplement 2N,O).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2N and 2O

claim: Lack of NCLX does not completely abrogate basal mitochondrial respiration, but negatively affects respiratory reserve.
source: These data suggest that lack of NCLX does not completely abrogate basal mitochondrial respiration, but negatively affects respiratory reserve, which is an indication of the cells ability to enhance mitochondrial respiration in response to higher energy demands.
evidence: Inferred from OCR data showing reduced spare respiratory capacity but maintained basal respiration

claim: MitoSOX dye intensity is significantly increased in all NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells, indicating increased mtROS.
source: MitoSOX dye intensity was significantly increased in all the NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells (Figure 4N,O), indicating increased mtROS in these cells.
evidence: Supported by MitoSOX flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4N and 4O

claim: Downregulation of NCLX with siRNA in HCT116, DLD1, and HT29 cells results in a significant increase in mtROS levels.
source: Using fluorescence microscopy, we also show that downregulation of NCLX with siRNA in HCT116 and DLD1 cells (and in another CRC cell line, HT29; See Figure 4—figure supplement 1M for evidence of SLC8B1 mRNA knockdown in HT29) results in a significant increase in mtROS levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2P,Q).
evidence: Supported by MitoSOX fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2P and 2Q

claim: Loss of NCLX decreases mtCa2+ extrusion, which affects mitochondrial cristae morphology and depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, leading to formation of autophagic vesicles and possibly mitophagy, decreased respiratory reserve capacity, and enhanced mtROS production.
source: The above data demonstrate that loss of NCLX decreases mtCa2+ extrusion, which affects mitochondrial cristae morphology and depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane, leading to formation of autophagic vesicles and possibly mitophagy, decreased respiratory reserve capacity, and enhanced mtROS production.
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple mitochondrial function assays

claim: GSEA analysis reveals that NCLX knockout drives the positive enrichment of pathways involved in hypoxia, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), TGF-β, pro-inflammatory, glycolysis, apoptosis and angiogenesis pathways.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) revealed that NCLX knockout drives the positive enrichment of pathways involved in hypoxia, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), TGF-β, pro-inflammatory, glycolysis, apoptosis and angiogenesis pathways, while negatively influencing gene expression of Myc targets, cell-cycle regulation, and oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 5A–G, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5A–G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F

claim: NCLX knockout negatively influences gene expression of Myc targets, cell-cycle regulation, and oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) revealed that NCLX knockout drives the positive enrichment of pathways involved in hypoxia, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), TGF-β, pro-inflammatory, glycolysis, apoptosis and angiogenesis pathways, while negatively influencing gene expression of Myc targets, cell-cycle regulation, and oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 5A–G, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 5A–G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–F

claim: GSEA analysis reveals that NCLX loss drives gene expression signatures associated with metastatic progression and inhibition of proliferation.
source: Thus, GSEA analysis revealed that NCLX loss drives gene expression signatures associated with metastatic progression and inhibition of proliferation, mirroring the phenotypic changes we observed following NCLX knockout and knockdown.
evidence: Summary conclusion from GSEA analysis correlating with observed phenotypes

claim: Gene expression signatures from NCLX loss are shared by the mesenchymal CMS4 CRC subtype, which is characterized by high rates of recurrence and predictive of poor patient outcome.
source: Interestingly, these gene expression signatures are shared by the mesenchymal CMS4 CRC subtype, which is characterized by high rates of recurrence, and predictive of poor patient outcome (Guinney et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison of GSEA results with known CMS4 subtype characteristics from Guinney et al., 2015

claim: Transcript levels of stem cell markers NANOG, Oct4, Sox2, and Foxo3 are significantly upregulated in NCLX KO cells.
source: In agreement with these findings, we found that transcript levels of stem cell markers NANOG, Oct4, Sox2, and Foxo3, as well as regulators of the glutathione synthesis pathway implicated in regulating these transcription factors in breast cancer, SLC7A11 and GCLM (Lu et al., 2015), were significantly upregulated in NCLX KO cells (Figure 5H–J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–O).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5H–J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–O

claim: Transcript levels of glutathione synthesis pathway regulators SLC7A11 and GCLM are significantly upregulated in NCLX KO cells.
source: In agreement with these findings, we found that transcript levels of stem cell markers NANOG, Oct4, Sox2, and Foxo3, as well as regulators of the glutathione synthesis pathway implicated in regulating these transcription factors in breast cancer, SLC7A11 and GCLM (Lu et al., 2015), were significantly upregulated in NCLX KO cells (Figure 5H–J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–O).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5H–J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–O

claim: NCLX KO clones acquire stem cell-like properties.
source: These data suggest that NCLX KO clones acquire stem cell-like properties.
evidence: Inferred from upregulation of stem cell markers in NCLX KO cells

claim: The IC50 of 5-FU for HCT116 NCLX KO cells (15 ± 1.2 µM) is significantly higher than for control HCT116 cells (8.2 ± 1.2 µM).
source: The IC50 of 5-FU for HCT116 NCLX KO cells (15 ± 1.2 µM) was significantly higher than the control HCT116 cells (8.2 ± 1.2 µM) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by IC50 measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: Treatment with 10 µM 5-FU causes a significant reduction in proliferation of control HCT116 and DLD1 cells at 24 and 72 hr.
source: The treatment with 10 µM 5-FU caused a significant reduction in proliferation of control HCT116 and DLD1 cells at 24 and 72 hr (Figure 5K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: Treatment of NCLX KO clones of HCT116 and DLD1 cells with 10 µM 5-FU yields only a marginal reduction in proliferation at 72 hr compared to non-treated NCLX KO clones.
source: Treatment of the NCLX KO clones of HCT116 (Figure 5K) and DLD1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) cells with 10 µM 5-FU yielded only a marginal reduction in proliferation at 72 hr as compared to non-treated NCLX KO clones, although this reduction was statistically significant for two NCLX KO clones of DLD1 cells at 72 hr time point (Clone#24 and #32; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: 5-FU causes a significant inhibition in migration of control HCT116 cells.
source: 5-FU also caused a significant inhibition in migration of control HCT116 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E), but did not affect the migratory capabilities of the NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and 1E

claim: 5-FU does not affect the migratory capabilities of NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells.
source: 5-FU also caused a significant inhibition in migration of control HCT116 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E), but did not affect the migratory capabilities of the NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and 1E

claim: HIF1α protein levels are strikingly increased in NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells in the absence of a hypoxic stimulus.
source: Hence, we measured HIF1α protein levels and found that HIF1α protein levels were strikingly increased in the NCLX KO clones of both HCT116 and DLD1 cells in the absence of a hypoxic stimulus (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A–D

claim: HIF1α protein levels are increased in HCT116 cells in which NCLX was knocked down with shRNA.
source: Similarly, HIF1α protein levels were also increased in HCT116 cells in which NCLX was knocked down with shRNA (NCLX KD; Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E and 6F

claim: HIF1α protein stabilization is significantly abrogated in NCLX KO cells when mtROS are scavenged using the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant mitoTEMPO.
source: Importantly, we were able to demonstrate that HIF1α protein stabilization was significantly abrogated in NCLX KO cells when mtROS were scavenged using the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant mitoTEMPO (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data with mitoTEMPO treatment shown in Figure 6G and 6H

claim: Assessment of AMPK and S6K1 phosphorylation reveals no difference between control HCT116 and clones of HCT116 NCLX KO cells.

claim: mTORC1 does not contribute to the regulation of HIF1α in response to NCLX ablation.

claim: NCLX KO cells compensate for their decreased respiratory reserve capacity by enhancing glycolytic pathways to meet their energy demands.

claim: Increased glycolysis is supporting migration of NCLX KO clones.
